about: Psalm 118 is an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one stanza for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with all eight verses of a stanza beginning on the same letter in the Hebrew. It is the longest psalm in the psalter, and nearly every verse of it speaks about one thing — God's law, called in turn law, testimony, statute, commandment, judgement, word. This stanza carries the letter HE. The Roman breviary says it at Terce on Sunday. Verse thirty-four — “Da mihi intelléctum, et scrutábor legem tuam” — is where this edition takes its name: a petition for understanding rather than for knowledge, and a promise to search rather than merely to read.

s01.translation: Set before me for a law, O Lord, the way of thy statutes, and I will seek it always.

s02.translation: Give me understanding, and I will search thy law, and I will keep it with my whole heart.

s03.translation: Lead me into the path of thy commandments, for that is the very thing I have wanted.

s04.translation: Incline my heart to thy testimonies, and not to greed.

s05.translation: Turn away my eyes, that they may not look on emptiness; give me life in thy way.

s06.translation: Establish thy word for thy servant, in thy fear.

s07.translation: Cut away the reproach I have feared, for thy judgements are delightful.

s08.translation: Behold, I have longed for thy commandments; give me life in thy justice.

w001.function: Not the object but a predicative accusative: the object is “viam” (w005), and “Legem” says what that way is to become. Latin sets a second accusative beside the object to say what a thing is being made into.

w002.function: Imperative. Not a request for a new law but that God should set it before the one praying — show it.

w004.function: Vocative: the whole stanza is addressed to God, and every “thy” in it is his.

w005.function: The object of “pone” (w002). The Greek psalter has a single verb here meaning to lay down as law; the Latin spreads it over “legem pone” and leaves the way as the thing laid down.

w006.function: Genitive plural. In the psalms iustificatiónes are not justification but statutes: what God has laid down as just.

w009.function: This edition states neither tense nor mood: the form is at once future indicative, “I will seek”, and present subjunctive, “let me seek”. Nothing in the sentence decides, so nothing is claimed. The same form returns in “custódiam” (w020).

w010.function: Feminine accusative. The nearest antecedent is “viam” (w005), but “Legem” (w001) is feminine too and the Latin does not decide between them.

w012.function: The verse this edition is named from begins here.

w015.function: After the petition “Da” (w012) the conjunction announces its promised result: give — and I will search.

w016.function: A future answering “Da” (w012), spoken like a vow: the gift of understanding comes first, then the work of searching.

w020.function: The same ambiguity as “exquíram” (w009): future indicative or present subjunctive. The unambiguous future “scrutábor” (w016) beside it tips the scale — but the form itself does not decide.

w024.function: Ablative with “in” (w022). In Hebrew idiom the heart is the seat of mind and will, not only of feeling — so the verse ends where it began: asking for understanding.

w026.function: Imperative; “Deduc” takes the shortened form without final -e, like “dic” and “duc”.

w029.function: Less than the “viam” (w005): a path worn rather than built.

w033.function: An intensive pronoun: not “it” but “that very one”, this and no other.

w034.function: A perfect: the choice is already made, not merely declared.

w035.function: The petition asks for a movement of the heart rather than for its conviction — tilt it, as a vessel is tilted.

w044.function: Accusative after “in” (w043): the direction the heart might lean instead.

w048.function: Opens a negative purpose clause, hence the subjunctive at “vídeant” (w049).

w049.function: Subjunctive after “ne” (w048): not a statement but the purpose for which the turning is asked.

w050.function: From vanus, empty. Not vanity as conceit but what is hollow and without substance.

w054.function: Imperative of vivífico — literally “make alive”, from vivus and fácere.

w056.function: From stare, to stand. The prayer asks that the word be set up so that it henceforth stands.

w059.function: In the psalms elóquium is nearly always God's word: the promise he has spoken.

w062.function: In the psalms nearly always the fear of God: not dread of punishment but the awe one stands in.

w064.function: Literally to prune round about. The petition is surgical, not gentle.

w065.function: Not shame felt inwardly but reproach thrown by others.

w067.function: Relative pronoun in the accusative, object of “suspicátus” (w068).

w068.function: Perfect participle of a deponent verb; with “sum” (w069) it forms one finite verb.

w069.function: Not a verb of its own: “suspicátus sum” is a single form, a deponent perfect — passive in shape, active in sense, so “I have feared” and not “I have been suspected”.

w071.function: Nominative plural; the verb “are” is understood, as Latin often leaves it.

w073.function: Predicate to the understood “are”. God's judgements are called delightful — not bearable but wanted.

w075.function: An inchoative verb: not “I desire” but “I came to desire”. The same root as concupiscence, here turned towards the commandments.

w079.function: From æquus, level. Not equality but what is even and right: the measure God judges by.

w081.function: The petition of verse 37 returns: the stanza opens and closes asking for life.
